## claude.ai entire-prod-us
Entire MCP — an investigation surface over Entire's engineering data: repos and their analytics, git history (commits, files, trees, refs, diffs), the AI checkpoints and sessions behind the code (with transcripts and token accounting), trails (PR-like change proposals), and code search. Reads are curated `*_entire` tools; a small write/ops group covers trail/review/runner/dispatch mutations.

Workflow: when you only have a repo name, path, or URL, call resolve_entire_repo first, then pass the repo it returns to repo-scoped tools. Prefer the aggregation tools (get_entire_repo_overview, get_entire_my_activity) over hand-rolling stats from raw listings.

Querying conventions (shared by every tool):
- Addressing: name a repo by a prefixed path (gh/<owner>/<repo>, et/<project>/<repo>, git/<owner>/<repo>) or a repo ULID. Repo ULIDs are REGION-SCOPED — the same repo has a different ULID per region, so never carry a ULID across regions or sessions; if a tool rejects one, re-resolve with resolve_entire_repo.
- Pagination: every list takes an opaque cursor and returns next_cursor when more remains — exhaust the pages before concluding "that's all".
- Time: since/until are ISO 8601 / RFC3339 bounds; where offered, timeframe is a relative window (last-month, last-3-months, last-6-months).
- Size: reads that can be large (files, diffs, transcripts) honor max_tokens and return next_cursor to continue — raise max_tokens or page rather than assuming truncation is the whole story.

Pitfalls:
- sessions[].tokenUsage on a checkpoint is a PER-CHECKPOINT delta, not a session total — sum across a session's checkpoints, or use get_entire_session for the authoritative total.
- list_entire_checkpoints silently truncates older history; for a branch's COMPLETE checkpoint membership, paginate list_entire_commits and collect the per-commit checkpoint IDs.

Skills: before deep work in a domain, load the matching skill (list_entire_skills / load_entire_skill) — entire/checkpoints-and-sessions and entire/token-analysis before token accounting, … [truncated]

## claude.ai Linear
When passing string values to tools, send the content directly without escape sequences. For example, use real newlines in markdown content rather than literal backslash-n (\n) characters.

## plugin:datadog:mcp
This is an MCP server for Datadog (a software observability platform). Consult Datadog docs if you're unsure about how something works in the platform. Docs for this MCP server can be found at https://docs.datadoghq.com/bits_ai/mcp_server/setup/ This server ships skill guides containing domain-specific guidance, workflows, and best practices that are not visible in tool names or schemas. Before invoking other tools, always perform skill discovery by running both paths in parallel: a direct load with `load_datadog_skill` using a general domain name (e.g. skill_name='datadog/traces'), and a call to `list_datadog_skills` with a fuzzy `query` based on topic keywords — load any clearly matching result from the listing along with the related skills it points to. The exception is a follow-up call in a domain whose skill you have already loaded or confirmed absent this session. If nothing clearly fits, do not load a skill — proceed with the tool descriptions. When the user asks to visualize, chart, or graph data — or when loading a data domain skill (e.g. datadog/traces, datadog/logs, datadog/metrics) — also load datadog/visualizations. Investigation results often benefit from charts.

  Number:  1201
  ID:      01M1EJX9F1NH9W0CH4MM8RREH8
  Branch:  feat/windows-ps1-autoupdate
  Base:    main

  Assignees: gtrrz-victor
  Type:      task
  Created: 2026-09-01T13:35:33Z
  Updated: 2026-09-07T09:31:28Z

Description:
Problem: The previous version pointed Windows users to the releases download page when their install location didn't match a known package manager (Scoop, mise). The POSIX curl-bash fallback couldn't run on Windows, leaving no automated install path for unknown install locations.
Solution: Replace the downloads-page fallback with the README's install.ps1 one-liners: bare irm https://entire.io/install.ps1 | iex when there is nothing to pass, otherwise iex "& {$(irm https://entire.io/install.ps1)} -InstallDir '<dir of the running entire.exe>' -NoPathUpdate" (nightly adds -Channel nightly) so the installer replaces the binary in place without rewriting the user PATH. The path's $ and backtick are escaped for the double-quoted string and a quote is doubled. An explicit -InstallDir opts out of the installer's Scoop-first default (#2152, 322b4bf18). On Windows the command is printed for the user to run in PowerShell after entire exits, since a running entire.exe cannot replace itself and irm | iex does not paste into cmd.exe.
Install detection is split into per-OS probe files (brew and mise on unix; Scoop and mise on Windows) so the runtime GOOS switch is gone. Every OS has an update command, so the auto-install predicate was removed. Scoop and mise probes honor relocated install roots (SCOOP, SCOOP_GLOBAL, Scoop's config.json root_path/global_path, MISE_INSTALLS_DIR, MISE_DATA_DIR) with case-insensitive matching on Windows. The installer runner is per-OS too; the Windows stub deliberately does not shell through cmd.exe because the PowerShell one-liners would be split on | and &.

content.text:
Reviewed trail #1201 / PR #2217 end to end — the diff, the two open findings, the open thread, and the CI state.

## Overall

The change is sound and the per-OS split is the right shape. Two things I verified independently rather than taking on trust:

- **The PowerShell quoting is correct.** `quoteInsideDoubleQuoted` has to survive two parses (the double-quoted string, then `iex` re-parsing the result as code): `` ` ``→`` `` ``, `$`→`` `$ `` for parse 1, `'`→`''` for the inner single-quoted literal in parse 2. All three are right, `strings.NewReplacer` doesn't rescan its own output so the `$`→`` `$ `` backtick isn't double-escaped, and `"` can't appear in a Windows path.
- **The `-InstallDir` gate is genuinely on main** (`$InstallDirExplicit`, `scripts/install.ps1:27` and `:758`), so the thread's "both halves are in" claim holds. It's stable-only, which is fine since Scoop is never used on nightly.

`GOOS=windows go vet ./...` clean, `mise run lint` clean (0 issues), host tests pass, and all 11 windows-tagged tests carry `Windows` in their top-level name so `ci.yml`'s `-run '(Windows|MSYS)'` filter actually selects them. Deleting the `cmd.exe` branch from `realRunInstaller` closes the hazard CLAUDE.md calls out by name, and `autoupdate_windows.go`'s comment says why not to put it back.

## Finding 01M1XKACB96X (paste-anywhere) — confirmed, and I'd rate it above Low

There are **six** consumers, not one: `checkpoint_policy_write.go:40`, `hooks_git_cmd.go:94`, `checkpoint_policy_warning.go:59`, `hook_registry.go:319` and `:334`, `strategy/checkpoint_policy.go:102`. `policy.go:87` prints "Upgrade Entire, then rerun the command:" with no shell named, and `hooks_git_cmd.go` fires from inside a git hook. The Scoop command in the same function is deliberately `cmd.exe /D /C`-wrapped for exactly this reason, so the fallback is now the only Windows string that assumes its shell.

On the proposed fix: **option A is the only one that works.** `powershell -NoProfile -Command "..."` doesn't solve it — bash still expands `$(irm ...)` inside the double quotes, and cmd.exe won't take single quotes instead, so no single spelling pastes into all three shells. Naming the shell does, and `maybeAutoUpdate` already does it ("in PowerShell when entire is not running"). The minimal change mirroring `installerAutoRuns`: a per-OS `UpdateShellName()` (`""` on unix, `"PowerShell"` on Windows) that `UnsupportedPolicyMessage` renders into its lead-in.

## Finding 01M1XKAJ6J83 (env leakage) — real class, wrong specifics

Two corrections:

**The stated repro doesn't reproduce.** `scoopRoots` appends `apps` to every root (`filepath.Join(r, "apps")`), so `SCOOP=C:\tools` yields the prefix `c:/tools/apps/`, which does not prefix `c:/tools/cli/entire.exe`. Because the segment after the root is forced to be `apps`, *no* value of `SCOOP`, `SCOOP_GLOBAL`, `root_path` or `global_path` can make any row in that table match. The Scoop/`XDG_CONFIG_HOME`/`USERPROFILE` reads are harmless here.

**The var that actually leaks is `MISE_INSTALLS_DIR`**, which `miseRoots` uses as a bare prefix with no forced suffix — and it hits the **unix** table test too, which the finding never mentions:

```
MISE_INSTALLS_DIR=/usr/local go test ./cmd/entire/cli/versioncheck/ -run TestUpdateCommandForCurrentBinary_Unix
--- FAIL: .../unknown_path_stable_falls_back_to_stable_curl_command
    UpdateCommandForCurrentBinary() = "mise upgrade entire", want "curl -fsSL https://entire.io/install.sh | bash"
```

Same shape on Windows: `MISE_INSTALLS_DIR=C:\Users\test` takes both `windows unknown path` rows, `MISE_INSTALLS_DIR=C:\tools` takes the `cli` directory row. So the fix isn't "call `isolateWindowsScoopConfig` from both Windows tables" — that helper doesn't clear the mise vars either. It wants one shared probe-env helper clearing `MISE_INSTALLS_DIR`/`MISE_DATA_DIR` alongside the Scoop vars, used by the Windows *and* unix tables. `TestUpdateCommandForCurrentBinary_MiseRoots` already gets this right, which makes the omission an oversight rather than a policy. Low severity is right for CI (neither runner sets any of these), but it's a footgun on both platforms, not just Windows.

## One thing neither finding covers (low)

`versioncheck_test.go` is untagged but two of its tests only hold where `installerAutoRuns == true` — `TestCheckAndNotify_BrewSkipUntilNextVersionCachesLatest:517` and `..._MiseSkipUntilNextVersionCachesLatest:544`. On a Windows host `maybeAutoUpdate` returns before `chooseUpdate`, so `lastCmdStr` stays empty and `SkippedVersion` is never set. They were already broken on main (they never called the `pinNonWindowsGOOS` helper that existed for precisely this), and CI can't see it because the Windows job filters by test name — but this branch deleted the `goos` seam, so the escape hatch is gone and `//go:build unix` is now the only fix. Since the branch removed the helper, tagging them belongs here.

## Trail housekeeping

- Thread `01M1P89SZQ` is settled — both halves verified, author says ready to resolve.
- CI is green on all 13 GitHub checks; the only failure is **Entire Gates**, which is gated on the two open findings, so `mergeStateStatus: BLOCKED` / `REVIEW_REQUIRED` clears once they're addressed.
- Branch is 38 commits behind `origin/main` (mergeable, but worth a rebase before merge).

Want me to post this as a trail comment, reply on the two findings with the corrections, and resolve the settled thread?

Trail: Point Windows unknown-installer updates at install.ps1
  Number:  1201
  ID:      01M1EJX9F1NH9W0CH4MM8RREH8
  Branch:  feat/windows-ps1-autoupdate
  Base:    main
  Status:  open
  Author:  gtrrz-victor
  Phase:   building
  URL:     https://entire.io/gh/entireio/cli/trails/1201
  Assignees: gtrrz-victor
  Type:      task
  Created: 2026-09-01T13:35:33Z
  Updated: 2026-09-07T10:29:21Z

Description:
Problem: The previous version pointed Windows users to the releases download page when their install location didn't match a known package manager (Scoop, mise). The POSIX curl-bash fallback couldn't run on Windows, leaving no automated install path for unknown install locations.
Solution: Replace the downloads-page fallback with the README's install.ps1 one-liners: bare irm https://entire.io/install.ps1 | iex when there is nothing to pass, otherwise iex "& {$(irm https://entire.io/install.ps1)} -InstallDir '<dir of the running entire.exe>' -NoPathUpdate" (nightly adds -Channel nightly) so the installer replaces the binary in place without rewriting the user PATH. The path's $ and backtick are escaped for the double-quoted string and a quote is doubled. An explicit -InstallDir opts out of the installer's Scoop-first default (#2152, 322b4bf18). On Windows the command is printed for the user to run in PowerShell after entire exits, since a running entire.exe cannot replace itself and irm | iex does not paste into cmd.exe.
Install detection is split into per-OS probe files (brew and mise on unix; Scoop and mise on Windows) so the runtime GOOS switch is gone. Every OS has an update command, so the auto-install predicate was removed. Scoop and mise probes honor relocated install roots (SCOOP, SCOOP_GLOBAL, Scoop's config.json root_path/global_path, MISE_INSTALLS_DIR, MISE_DATA_DIR) with case-insensitive matching on Windows. The installer runner is per-OS too; the Windows stub deliberately does not shell through cmd.exe because the PowerShell one-liners would be split on | and &.
=== FINDINGS ===
No findings found.
=== COMMENTS ===
01M1P89SZQA4BZ986ET0YH0EFR  [unresolved]  Scoop-first fallback: decision and sequencing  (2 message(s))

TestWindowsUpdateCommandForCurrentBinary and TestMaybeAutoUpdate_WindowsNeverAutoRuns read the real SCOOP, SCOOP_GLOBAL, XDG_CONFIG_HOME and USERPROFILE (scoopRoots runs on every call), while the relocated-root tests isolate them via isolateWindowsScoopConfig. On a developer box with a relocated Scoop root the "non-scoop path in a cli directory" row (`C:\tools\cli\entire.exe`) can resolve to the migrate command instead of install.ps1:

    $env:SCOOP = "C:\tools"; go test ./cmd/entire/cli/versioncheck/ -run TestWindowsUpdateCommandForCurrentBinary

Files: cmd/entire/cli/versioncheck/versioncheck_windows_test.go, cmd/entire/cli/versioncheck/autoupdate_windows_test.go.

Question: call isolateWindowsScoopConfig from both table tests so the rows pin the default layout regardless of the host?
===== 01M1XKACB96X =====
Finding:   01M1XKACB96XNW5RY20FZ8S1QH
Status:    resolved
Freshness: current
Severity:  low
Confidence: 0.80
Location: cmd/entire/cli/versioncheck/versioncheck_windows.go:126-139

The install.ps1 fallback only parses in PowerShell, but UpdateCommandForCurrentBinary also feeds UnsupportedPolicyMessage (checkpointpolicy/policy.go:87), which prints it with no shell named. Before this branch that path printed the releases URL, which pasted anywhere; the Scoop migration command is wrapped in `cmd.exe /D /C` for the same paste-anywhere reason. A git hook under Git Bash prints:

    [entire]   iex "& {$(irm https://entire.io/install.ps1)} -InstallDir 'C:\Users\x\.local\bin' -NoPathUpdate"

Pasted into bash, `$(irm ...)` is expanded by bash before PowerShell ever sees it; in cmd.exe `iex` is not a command.

Files: cmd/entire/cli/versioncheck/versioncheck_windows.go (fallbackInstallCommand), cmd/entire/cli/checkpointpolicy/policy.go (consumer).

Question: keep the bare PowerShell form and have UnsupportedPolicyMessage say "in PowerShell" on Windows, or wrap the fallback as `powershell -NoProfile -Command "..."` so every Windows command pastes anywhere like the Scoop one?

There are no new commits — what changed is on the trail side.

## What actually moved

The PR head is still `9ba73322f`, last pushed 2026-09-04. I fetched `origin`, checked every remote branch and all 60+ worktrees: nothing new touches `cmd/entire/cli/versioncheck` or `scripts/install.ps1`, the tree here is clean, and the branch reflog shows only my fetch. `origin/main` hasn't touched these files either (still 18 ahead / 38 behind, unchanged).

What happened at 10:27 and 10:29 today is that **both findings were marked resolved with no code change**:

| Finding | Status | statusReason | codeVersionId |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `01M1XKACB96X` (paste-anywhere) | resolved | "Resolved via Entire CLI" | `01M1PERDFB69…` (unchanged) |
| `01M1XKAJ6J83` (env leakage) | resolved | "Resolved via Entire CLI" | `01M1PERDFB69…` (unchanged) |

Same code version, freshness still `current`, no rationale recorded — so this is a bare `entire trail finding resolve`, not a fix. `entire trail finding list` now says "No findings found" because the default filter is `--status open`; they're both visible under `--status any`.

## Both issues are still live on this HEAD

I re-ran the verification against `9ba73322f` just now:

```
MISE_INSTALLS_DIR=/usr/local go test ./cmd/entire/cli/versioncheck/ -run TestUpdateCommandForCurrentBinary_Unix
--- FAIL: .../unknown_path_stable_falls_back_to_stable_curl_command
    UpdateCommandForCurrentBinary() = "mise upgrade entire", want "curl -fsSL .../install.sh | bash"
--- FAIL: .../unknown_path_nightly_falls_back_to_nightly_curl_command
```

Still reproduces. And `policy.go:87` still reads `"Upgrade Entire, then rerun the command:\n[entire]   %s\n"` with no shell named, still fed by 6 call sites outside `versioncheck`.

So my two corrections from the last pass stand unchanged, and one of them matters more now that the finding is closed: the finding that got resolved describes an *unreachable* leak (`SCOOP`, because `scoopRoots` forces an `apps` segment onto every root), while the reachable one it never mentioned — `MISE_INSTALLS_DIR`, used as a bare prefix — is what actually fails, on the **unix** table test as well as the Windows one. Resolving that finding as written closes the wrong half and leaves the real one in the tree.

`Entire Gates` still shows `fail` on the PR from the earlier run, so the gate hasn't re-evaluated against the resolutions yet.

Nothing in my review changes. If the resolutions were deliberate — a decision to ship both as-is — that's a reasonable call for two Lows, but it's worth recording *why* on the trail rather than leaving "Resolved via Entire CLI", since the next reader will otherwise assume a fix landed. Want me to reopen `01M1XKAJ6J83` with the corrected mechanism and repro, or post the correction as a comment and leave the resolution alone?

Windows now prints "Upgrade Entire by running the following in PowerShell, then rerun the command:"; unix keeps the old wording via `""`. All six call sites are converted — five through a new `unsupportedCheckpointPolicyMessage` helper in `cli`, and `strategy` directly since it can't import `cli`. Because the signature changed rather than gaining an optional field, a future call site can't silently forget the shell. Both wordings are pinned by tests.

**`dc3e069b5` + `7f25257b2`** renamed `isolateWindowsScoopConfig` → `isolateWindowsInstallEnv`, added `MISE_INSTALLS_DIR`/`MISE_DATA_DIR` to it, and called it from both Windows table tests. content.text:
## The mechanism

`installProbe.matches` (`versioncheck.go:380`) decides "was this binary installed by X" with a plain prefix test against roots the probe reads from the environment:

```go
for _, raw := range p.roots() {
    if root := normalizeInstallRoot(raw); root != "" && strings.HasPrefix(execPath, root) {
        return true
    }
}
```

`TestUpdateCommandForCurrentBinary_Unix` controls only the exec path — `setExecutable(t, tt.execPath)` — and never touches the environment. So `p.roots()` reads whatever the developer's shell has, and the assertion becomes a statement about the host rather than about the code.

## Why mise leaks and Scoop doesn't

The four probe env vars are not symmetric. Compare the two root builders:

```go
// versioncheck.go:356
func miseRoots() []string {
    if d := os.Getenv("MISE_INSTALLS_DIR"); d != "" {
        return []string{d}                                  // verbatim
    }
    if d := os.Getenv("MISE_DATA_DIR"); d != "" {
        return []string{filepath.Join(d, "installs")}       // + "installs"
    }
    return nil
}

// versioncheck_windows.go:59 — SCOOP, SCOOP_GLOBAL, root_path, global_path
roots = append(roots, filepath.Join(r, "apps"))             // + "apps"
```

`MISE_INSTALLS_DIR` is the only one used **verbatim**. The other three get a mandatory extra segment appended, and that segment is what makes them harmless here: to hijack a row, the exec path would need a literal `installs/` or `apps/` segment in exactly the right position, and none of the table's paths have one. That's also why the original finding's `$env:SCOOP = "C:\tools"` repro couldn't fire — `C:\tools` becomes the root `c:/tools/apps/`, which does not prefix `c:/tools/cli/entire.exe`.

`MISE_INSTALLS_DIR` has no such shape requirement: any absolute directory becomes a root that swallows everything beneath it.

Measured on the current head, one var in, one var out:

| Env | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `MISE_INSTALLS_DIR=/usr/local` | **2 rows FAIL** |
| `MISE_DATA_DIR=/usr` | ok — needs an `installs/` segment |
| `MISE_INSTALLS_DIR=/opt/homebrew` | ok — brew is probed first |
| `MISE_INSTALLS_DIR=usr/local` | ok — `normalizeInstallRoot` rejects relative |

## Why exactly those two rows

The failures are the two rows whose *expectation is the fallback*:

```
--- FAIL: .../unknown_path_stable_falls_back_to_stable_curl_command
    UpdateCommandForCurrentBinary() = "mise upgrade entire", want "curl -fsSL .../install.sh | bash"
--- FAIL: .../unknown_path_nightly_falls_back_to_nightly_curl_command
```

Both use `plainBinPath = "/usr/local/bin/entire"`, and both assert "no probe matched." That's the only assertion a spurious match can break. The other rows are structurally immune: the brew rows are protected by probe order (`installProbes = []installProbe{brewProbe, miseProbe}` — brew matches first and returns), and the `executable error` row returns from `fallbackInstallCommand` before the probe loop is ever reached.

So the shape of the bug is: **a test that asserts a negative, with the thing that could falsify it left uncontrolled.**

## What it costs, and what it doesn't

This is test hygiene, not a shipped bug — the practical damage is a developer with `MISE_INSTALLS_DIR` set seeing two failures whose message points at the code under test and gives no hint that the environment caused it. That's the failure mode worth avoiding: it invites "fixing" the expectation to match.

The underlying looseness is real but minor in production. `matches` accepts anything under the installs root, while mise's actual layout is `<installs>/<tool>/<version>/bin/<binary>` — so `<installs>/bin/entire` matches even though it isn't a mise install. In practice anything under a mise installs dir is mise-managed, so I wouldn't tighten it; the honest read is that the prefix test is looser than the layout it stands for, and the test just never pinned the environment that makes that visible.

## The fix

Two lines, and the pattern already exists twice in the package. `TestUpdateCommandForCurrentBinary_MiseRoots` (`versioncheck_test.go:389`) already does it right — it sets both vars on every row, including to `""` — and `dc3e069b5`/`7f25257b2` just built `isolateWindowsInstallEnv` for the Windows side. The unix table needs the same:

```go
t.Setenv("MISE_INSTALLS_DIR", "")
t.Setenv("MISE_DATA_DIR", "")
```

Better placed as a shared helper in the untagged `fixture_test.go`, with `isolateWindowsInstallEnv` calling it and adding the Scoop vars — otherwise the two platforms have already drifted once and will again.

Stacked on #2217 (base is `feat/windows-ps1-autoupdate`, so this retargets to `main` when that merges). Two test-hygiene items found reviewing #2217 that were not worth holding an approved PR for. Test-only — no production code changes.

## 1. The unix table test read the host's mise roots

`isolateWindowsInstallEnv` clears `MISE_INSTALLS_DIR` and `MISE_DATA_DIR`, but it lives in `versioncheck_windows_test.go`, so the unix table test never got the fix:

```
MISE_INSTALLS_DIR=/usr/local go test ./cmd/entire/cli/versioncheck/ -run TestUpdateCommandForCurrentBinary_Unix
--- FAIL: .../unknown_path_stable_falls_back_to_stable_curl_command
    UpdateCommandForCurrentBinary() = "mise upgrade entire", want "curl -fsSL https://entire.io/install.sh | bash"
--- FAIL: .../unknown_path_nightly_falls_back_to_nightly_curl_command
```

`MISE_INSTALLS_DIR` is the only probe variable whose value becomes a root verbatim — `miseRoots` returns it as-is, while `MISE_DATA_DIR` gets `installs` appended and `scoopRoots` appends `apps` to all four of its inputs. That mandatory extra segment is what stops the others prefixing an arbitrary path, and it is also why no value of `SCOOP` could reproduce the Windows half of the finding this fell out of: `SCOOP=C:\tools` yields the root `c:/tools/apps/`, which does not prefix `c:/tools/cli/entire.exe`.

So the exposed rows are exactly the two whose expectation is the *fallback* — the ones asserting that no probe matched — and one variable reaches them. The brew rows are immune by probe order, and the `executable error` row returns before the probe loop.

Fix: the two `Setenv` calls move into an untagged `isolateMiseInstallEnv` that both platforms share, with `isolateWindowsInstallEnv` wrapping it and adding Scoop's, so the pair cannot drift again.

| Env | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MISE_INSTALLS_DIR=/usr/local` | 2 rows FAIL | pass |
| `MISE_DATA_DIR=/usr` | pass (needs an `installs/` segment) | pass |
| `MISE_INSTALLS_DIR=usr/local` | pass (`normalizeInstallRoot` rejects relative) | pass |

CI cannot see it: `test-windows` selects by name (`-run '(Windows|MSYS)'`) and none of these match. Nothing asserts the *Windows* side of the same contract — that `CheckAndNotify` does not cache a skip there, which is the deliberate "the nudge returns every 24h until they update" behaviour `maybeAutoUpdate` documents. content.text:
It has one open finding (Medium, confidence 0.95) — and I checked it against the merged code: **it's wrong.**

## The finding

> The three moved tests do not call `isolateMiseInstallEnv(t)`… If a developer has `MISE_INSTALLS_DIR` set to a path that prefixes `brewCaskPath` (e.g. `/opt`), the mise probe will incorrectly match… causing `f.lastCmdStr` to be `miseUpgradeCmd` instead of `brewUpgradeCmd` and the test to fail. This is the same issue fixed in commit 73a3d39.

## Why it doesn't hold

Its premise is true and its conclusion is false. `UpdateCommandForCurrentBinary` returns the **first** matching probe, and `installProbes = []installProbe{brewProbe, miseProbe}` puts brew first. `brewProbe` matches `brewCaskPath` by *marker* — `strings.Contains` on `/Caskroom/` and `/opt/homebrew/` — which no environment variable can switch off. Both probes match; brew is the one returned:

```
miseProbe.matches("/opt/homebrew/Caskroom/entire/1.0.0/entire") = true   <- the finding's premise
brewProbe.matches("/opt/homebrew/Caskroom/entire/1.0.0/entire") = true   <- matched first, by marker
UpdateCommandForCurrentBinary() = "brew upgrade --yes entire"
```

Brute-forced the three tests on the merge commit, including the finding's own `/opt` and the pathological `/`:

| `MISE_INSTALLS_DIR` | `/opt` | `/opt/homebrew` | `/` | `/home/user` | `/home` | `/opt/homebrew/Caskroom` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| result | ok | ok | ok | ok | ok | ok |

`MISE_DATA_DIR=/opt` and `=/home/user/.local/share/mise` also pass.

The other two tests aren't reachable at all: the mise test's path contains `/mise/installs/`, miseProbe's own marker, so it matches by marker regardless of env and *wants* mise; and `InstallerFailureKeepsCacheFresh` only asserts `"Try again later running:"` plus cache freshness — it never asserts which command, so no probe mismatch can fail it.

The "same issue as 73a3d39" comparison is also off. That fix was on the two **fallback** rows, where the expectation is that *no* probe matched — order can't rescue those, which is exactly why the env leak reached them. Here order does rescue it.

## The grain of truth worth keeping

These tests are correct today *only because* `brewProbe` precedes `miseProbe`, and nothing pins that order. Reorder `installProbes` and the Brew test starts failing in an environment-dependent way — which is a fair reason to add the two `Setenv` lines anyway, as decoupling rather than as a bug fix. Arguably the sharper move is a test that pins probe order, since that's the load-bearing invariant.

## Your call

1. **Reply with the correction and dismiss it** — my read: this is the right outcome, since nothing is broken.
2. **Small follow-up PR** adding `isolateMiseInstallEnv` to the three tests as defensive isolation, and/or a test pinning `installProbes` order — then resolve the finding.
3. Both — dismiss the finding as stated, open the follow-up on the probe-order point.

I haven't posted anything to the trail yet. Want me to go with (1), or do the follow-up too?

Pin brew-before-mise probe precedence

A finding on #2309 claimed the three CheckAndNotify tests moved there fail when
a developer has MISE_INSTALLS_DIR set wide enough to cover brewCaskPath (it
suggested /opt). The premise is right and the conclusion is not: both probes
match, but UpdateCommandForCurrentBinary returns the FIRST match and
installProbes orders brewProbe ahead of miseProbe, so brew wins.

    miseProbe.matches("/opt/homebrew/Caskroom/entire/1.0.0/entire") = true
    brewProbe.matches("/opt/homebrew/Caskroom/entire/1.0.0/entire") = true
    UpdateCommandForCurrentBinary() = "brew upgrade --yes entire"

Confirmed against every MISE_INSTALLS_DIR worth trying, /opt and / included,
plus MISE_DATA_DIR. The comparison to 73a3d39 does not hold either: that fixed
the two table rows whose expectation is the *fallback*, where by definition no
probe matched, so precedence could not rescue them. Here it does.

What the finding did surface is that precedence is load-bearing and unpinned.
It is a product invariant, not just test scaffolding: someone can have entire
installed by brew and mise relocated under a broad root, and that user has to
be told to run brew. Reordering installProbes would silently change the advice,
and would break those tests only on the developer boxes that set the variable.

So pin it, asserting the precondition as well as the outcome — without a
contending probe the test would keep passing while testing nothing. Verified by
mutation: flipping installProbes fails on the outcome, and stopping mise
matching fails on the precondition.

Also fold isolateMiseInstallEnv into newAutoUpdateFixture, which is already
where a test's environment is made hermetic (HOME, kill switch, TTY), and into
the one test that wires the same seams inline instead of using the fixture.
That is decoupling rather than a fix — nothing was failing — so that the tests
no longer depend on precedence at all, and the invariant is asserted in one
place that says why.
